problem gambling, but today they do not. They are not exercising their consciences.
John Key has systematically and deliberate ly undermined basic New Zealand values
through this dodgy deal. It is shameful legi slation, and the National members who are
today being prevented from exer cising their consciences know this. This bill is morally
wrong. This bill is morally bankrupt. The Labour Party is disgusted by this bill. Labour
will not be bullied out of making changes to gambling law because of what this
Government says. If Labour sees gambling ha rm when it is in Government, it will
legislate to deal with gambling harm. John Key cannot get away with this dodgy,
tawdry deal. It is morally bankrupt and the Labour Party is utterly opposed to it.
11984 New Zealand International Conve ntion Centre Bill 11 Jul 2013

items.speaker: JONATHAN YOUNG
items.text: Well, the previous Labour
Government has a significant convention centre under its belt. Helen Clark speaks from
the past. She said that the Auckland S kycity has “pumped $140 million into its new
Convention Centre, and Auckland City has rebranded and upgraded its conventions
facilities.” She says it is a good thing. Mark Burton, who was the Minister  of Internal
Affairs at the time, said: “The potential gains from this  are widespread—not only for
Skycity but for the Auckland city and regi on, the tourism industry, and the whole of
New Zealand.” Oh, my—have they not ch anged their tune! The Labour Mayor of
Auckland, Len Brown, agrees, too. He welcom ed the “significant opportunities that a
national convention centre will bring to Auckland both in terms of jobs and wider
economic growth.”
We understand very, very clearly that th ere are issues around gambling harm and
harm minimisation. That is why we have  placed upon Skycity a very, very strong
obligation and requirement to introduce further, substantial harm reduction measures. In
fact, Associate Professor Paul Delfabbro from the University of Adelaide, who works in
the psychology department, recently de scribed Skycity’s Host Responsibility
programme as one of the most rigorous in the world.
It is important to understand that these things are also on the Government’s mind,
and, because of that, there are very stringent obligations placed upon Skycity in order to
minimise gambling harm. Under the agreem ent Skycity will have to introduce a
predictive modelling tool that analyses data to identify players at risk of problem
gambling, as well as a voluntary pre-commitme nt system where players can elect to
restrict the amount of time they play or the amount they spend. Skycity will also have to
introduce player identification requiremen ts when amounts over $500 are being put on
to, or cashed from, ticket-in, ticket-out machin es in non-restricted areas. As well, it is
doubling the number of Host Responsibility specialists to deliver 24-hour, 7-day-a-week
coverage.
Arguably, Skycity will be better equipped to deal with problem gamblers because of
this bill than it would be w ithout it, because it will put into  place industry best practice.
I am not a gambler, but this place is full of gamblers. Right now there are bets going on
in this House on who is going to be the winning horse we aring the red tunic, and games
of Russian roulette are being played in the Labour caucus. But I want to say that this bill
is going to be good for New Zealand, and at the same time we are going to minimise the
impacts and the harm upon people of gambling.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Just before I call the next
member, I advise the House that this is a split Labour call, and I will ring the bell with 1
minute remaining. I call the Hon Clayton Cosgrove.

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: Before I make my substantive comments
in this speech, I want to make a persona l comment. The personal comment is that, in
respect of Skycity, I attended a corporate box function—as is well known. I want to say
to the House in all seriousness that it may co me as a shock to some people here, but,
like other members, I have attended and r eceived hospitality from Federated Farmers
occasionally. I have received and attended hospitality from Sky TV occasionally, and, I
have to say in seriousness, I have been to  the annual function of Saunders Unsworth at
some times over the years, although I suspect that the invitation may not come this year.
I say in all seriousness that one engages with  groups and entities as a member of this
House, and one makes judgments as to the rights and sometimes the wrongs of those
engagements with entities and groups. I take  responsibility for both the right judgments
and—hopefully, not that often—the wrong judgments. I take responsibility. But I say
this: my vote is not for sale. My vote cannot  be bought. My vote will never be bought. I
11 Jul 2013 New Zealand Internatio nal Convention Centre Bill 11985
say with respect to the House that my commen ts, I think, are appropriate before I get to
the New Zealand International Convention Centre Bill.
The problem with this bill is the follo wing. You can understand a private sector
organisation like Skycity wanting to get the best deal it can under any legal
circumstances. That is how businesses proceed in terms of maximising their
profitability. The problem, though, is that even though John Key is  a product of that
same private sector where things are done differently and there are different processes—
because there are commercial arrangements and private sector moneys involved—there
is a big difference when you are dealing with public money, with legislation and
regulation, and with taxpayers’ money, and when you are charged as a Government and
as a Prime Minister with working in the in terests of all people. And though John Key in
his private sector capacity may even in a legal sense have been able to expedite
decisions without a lot of due process, in a legal sense even without due process, to get
the deal done, get it done fast, and move it ahead, the difficulty when you are a Prime
Minister and when you are charged in Govern ment with guarding the public purse and
the public well-being is that you must have transparency, you must have openness, and
you must observe proper due process, espe cially in tender pr ocesses. You cannot
express a preference for one group against anot her. You must leave key decisions to be
delegated to officials to keep  them out of the sticky finge rs of politicians and avoid
some of the challenges and allegations th at Mr Grant Robertson has put to the
Government. You must observe those public sector processes.
The difficulty Mr Key has with this dodgy deal—and from the taxpayers’ point of
view it is; you cannot blame the Skycity boys  for having a crack a nd, forgive the pun,
rolling the dice—is that he has failed to gua rd the well-being of the taxpayers. He has
been criticised by the Auditor-General for a lack of due process, even though in his own
mind he keeps telling himself that he wa s totally vindicated—though the Skycity report
says otherwise. He has done this and done the deal, whether it be with the film industry
at the cost of selling legisla tion, or whether it be this in a dodgy, non-transparent, and
underhand way. He has done it simply for po litical motives and political motivation.
The Government may cry jobs, a nd we are all in favour  of jobs. It may cry that it wants
to grow incomes for people, and we are all in  favour of that. But you have got to do it
openly and you have got to do it fairly. It cannot be a dodgy deal done at midnight with
high-level Government ministerial interventi on that has been deemed inappropriate. I
will oppose this legislation for those reasons. Mr Key has to learn that he is a Prime
Minister. He is not in the private sector . He is not dealing with his own dough or
company dough; he is dealing with taxpayers ’ money and taxpayers’ welfare. There is
such a thing as the public interest, the taxpayer interest, and he is charged with guarding
that. This legislation and his conduct fail those critical tests.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: I think there are some things
that I too should put on the record. I think in 2009 I accepted a couple of glasses of wine
from Skycity at one of its lower bars, in 2011 I went to a test match as part of the Rugby
World Cup with Skycity, and earlier this year, in 2013, I accepted a cup of coffee and a
muffin with one of its lobbyists when we were discu ssing this legislation, the New
Zealand International Convention Centre Bill. I am, however, reminded of the statement
of the late California State Treasurer “Big  Daddy” Unruh, and that is: “If you can’t eat
their food, drink their booze, …”—there is another phrase that has to do with the
relationship with women, which I will not read out—“and then vote against them, you
have no business being [in Parliament].” That is the case. I just want to say that if
people cannot have a proper policy discussi on and at the end of that say “No, we
disagree.”—as I have on a number of occas ions with Skycity—and tell people that you
11986 New Zealand International Conve ntion Centre Bill 11 Jul 2013
are against something, and then come here and vote against it, then we have not got a
proper democracy.
I am adamantly opposed to this legislation. My view is that gambling using any form
of pokies was originally a mistake. I think that in allowing it, Peter Tapsell—probably
without any right of legislation, without a ny right and proper regulation, back when he
was Minister of Internal Affairs in the early 1980s—was wrong. I am still convinced
that it is wrong. I voted the wrong way on the casino legislation when it was set up
originally, and that is something that I am now ashamed of. It is my view that that
casino should not have been set up, and my view that the harm that is  caused to tens of
thousands of families is something that this Parliament, and people of my generation in
this Parliament, have to take responsibility for. What I will not do is support in any way
legislation that will make it worse.
Pokies and gambling tables cause immense harm to families. People gamble much
more, in some cases, than they can afford to. They lose their houses, they lose their
families, and, in extreme cases, they lose thei r lives as a result of this evil. And for the
Prime Minister to trade this loss of families, this loss of houses, and this loss of lives for
a convention centre is, in my opinion, morally  bankrupt, and the way that it has been
done is, effectively, corrupt. The Prime Minist er wrote on a piece of paper to finalise a
deal with Skycity. He wrote on a piece of paper and breached everything that is ethical
about having proper tenders and proper arrangements in making Government deals. The
Prime Minister of New Zealand lowered the standards of our democracy, and the ethics
and the integrity and th e transparency that we expect in  New Zealand, and this bill is a
result of it.
And I say to Jonathan Young, who was the National Party speaker who preceded me,
shame on you. Jonathan, I know that you know better. I know that you know that people
will die as a result of th is bill. I know, Mr Young, that  in your heart and in your
conscience you do not support it, and I say sh ame on you for standing up to support this
grubby bill.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I call the honourable
member Metiria Turei. Tēnā koe. Kei te pēhea koe?

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: Tino pai, Mr Speaker. T ēnā koe. “But
gambling is not just the scourge of my communities. We all know that there are
teachers, there are lawyers, and there are even  politicians who gamble. So let us not say
that this is a problem defined to one area, but across the country. It  is also personal
because I have had numerous constituents come  into my electorate office in Onehunga
in Maungakiekie, and I have seen the broken relationships. I have seen kids who have
gone without the essentials, the broken familie s, and the broken relationships. It affects
our communities right across this country.”—so said Peseta Sam Lotu-Iiga last night in
this House, and I agree with him. I agree with him 100 percent, and so do thousands of
New Zealanders. So my plea to all of my parliamentary colleagues today is: “Do not
vote for this bill.”—the New Zealand International Convention Centre Bill.
Today we have a rare opportunity to vote with our conscience on a bill that we all
know grates so deeply, and it grates because it is wrong. It  is wrong to sell the law to
Skycity so that Skycity and no one else can make millions of dollars off the misery of
problem gamblers, their families, their childr en, and their communities. It is wrong to
use the authority of this House to excuse Skycity for 35 years from the Gambling Act,
the Act that constrains the harm of gamb ling by stemming its growth. It is wrong to
know that increasing gambling at Skycity will  produce measurable, predictable harm to
people who can least afford to be harmed but to choose to do so a nyway. It is wrong to
subvert the very foundation of our law—the law that says that we are all equal before
11 Jul 2013 New Zealand Internatio nal Convention Centre Bill 11987
it—to confer on Skycity a special privilege that  the rest of us simply do not have. That
is wrong, and there is no more simple way to put it.
People’s lives have been destroyed by ga mbling and by Skycity. Every few months
we hear another story about another busin ess that has gone under, about people who
have become sick, their lives destroyed, w ho have stolen from their employers, have
harmed or abandoned their children, and have even harmed themselves because of that
place. So please do not use this one vote you have today to make Skycity bigger, more
rapacious, and more damaging than it is alre ady. We all have the power today to stop
that from happening.
I would add to that a concern about the natu re of Skycity. Today, in fact just a few
moments ago, I saw a press report on Skycity and a comment that it made, where it is in
effect threatening MPs today, saying that if MPs choose to deny this legislation and vote
it down, Skycity will take its money—hundreds of millions of dollars, says Nigel
Morrison—and spend it overseas. So it is effectively attempting to threaten MPs—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Good riddance.

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: —good riddance, I agree, Mr Ma llard—by saying that it will
remove its business and take it elsewhere, in a deliberate attempt to use its financial
power to influence the votes of members of Parliament. We are seeing that happen right
as we speak today with this release from Skycity.
John Key would have us all believe, despite  the fact that these gambling extensions
breach the law and despite the demonstrable ha rm that they bring, that these extensions
are necessary for Auckland to get ahead on jobs. Well, of course, Auckland, as we
know, is much, much better than that. Au cklanders are creativ e, innovative, and
imaginative, and they are better than this dirty deal of expanding a casino and placing a
casino monument—plonked right in the middle of their beautiful city.
The other fallacy that John Key and Steven J oyce would have us believe is that jobs
should come at any cost, but that is just simply not true. Not only are the numbers
false—there are not those numbers of jobs th at they say, and if you look at any of the
reports it is clear that they are overestima ting the jobs—but jobs do not come at any
cost, and they most certainly must not come  at the cost of 6,500 children who, Joyce’s
own officials warn, will be harmed by this bill. That is 6,500 children who the officials
say will be at risk of not being fed and clothe d properly as a result of this bill. This is
not my information. I did not produce this inform ation. This is information that is in the
Government’s own, albeit heavily edited, care fully redacted, and se lectively released
documents. It is information that it has produced and has known about.
The jobs claim of Steven Joyce is untrue. One need only look at the reports to show
that that is the case. Even the $90 million cl aim that is being made by Steven Joyce is
untrue. The Ministry of Busi ness, Innovation and Employment reports that its analysis
shows that 72 percent of th at money will go to Skycity  through the hotel and through
the convention centre. So very little of that $90 million is going anywhere near outside
the Skycity boundaries.
Steven Joyce and John Key say that because we cannot know for sure exactly how
many people are to be harmed or how they will be harmed by the increased gambling
that this bill brings, the risk to those pe ople or the risk of th at harm is somehow
irrelevant. Joyce claimed yesterday that the regulatory impact statement said that putting
a precise cost on the potential increase is diffi cult. Well, yes, it does say that, but it also
goes on to say why it is difficult to put a precise cost on the harms. It says: “Reportedly,
only a fraction of those who are affected by pr oblem gambling seek help and the cost of
the intervention services is in any case only a fraction of the cost (harms) associated
with problem gambling (such as suicide; fam ily violence; children inadequately clothed
and fed, and other examples of deprivation and poor parenting; costs to the justice
11988 New Zealand International Conve ntion Centre Bill 11 Jul 2013
system, to businesses, and to community groups of gambling-related crime, lost
productivity etc.).” That is what it says in the regulatory impact statement.
All of those harms are identified as being real, and the risk of those harms being real.
Yes, it is difficult to quantify the cost, but that does not mean that those harms do not
exist. It does not mean those harms are irreleva nt to this debate. In fact, it raises serious
questions when this bill is proceeding knowing that those harms are a risk and when Mr
Joyce today confirmed that he has made no attempt to find the real evidence behind that.
No, he did not seek any advice about whether mo re children would be left in cars in the
Skycity car-park, even though we know that that happens. No, he has not assessed the
risk of increased fraud for those businesse s that we know will suffer from theft and
fraud—usually by people who own or are seni or in those businesses—as a result of
problem gambling. No, he has not sought any advice on the risk to charities—charities
that not only receive funding from the members of the pub lic but also receive funding
from Government—of that money being st olen, when we know that more than 50
percent of the money that is stolen from charities is stolen to fuel problem gambling.
These are the facts that we know. This is the information that we have available to
us, but John Key and Steven Joyce have de liberately refused to investigate that
information because if they do not know, then  they can pretend it does not exist. Yet
that harm will be experienced by thousands of New Zealanders and, more important, by
thousands of their children.
I am going to end by quoting a member of  this House who fought against the 1997
Casino Control (Moratorium) Amendment B ill 15 years ago. He said: “We are talking
about a problem that we all own. We cannot  just sweep the probl em under the carpet
because we believe in free enterprise. We  cannot just sweep the problem under the
carpet because we think it is an  individual’s right to throw th e dice, to play blackjack ...
We have a problem in this c ountry, and it is the addiction of gambling. It creates havoc
amongst families, be they M āori, be they P ākehā. It creates a problem, and we need a
Parliament with the strength and courage to face up to that problem, and face up to it we
will.”, and “We have a problem, and those pe ople who vote in favour of this Bill are on
the side of the angels, and those who vote ag ainst this legislati on are on the side of
evil.” Thank you, Mr Tau Henare, for those wise words.

items.speaker: Peseta SAM LOTU-IIGA
items.text: Talofa lava. I want to
acknowledge the Minister for Economic Develo pment, Steven Joyce, for bringing the
New Zealand International Convention Centre  Bill to the House. We have heard the
debate. The bill is a trade-off—it is a trade-off in terms of the positives that we get from
jobs, from tourism, from opportunities, and from the economic benefits that this bill will
produce. We also understand, and we know, that gambling is a legally permitted activity
in this country and that there are some spin-off effects that are detrimental to some
individuals and some families.
But let me talk about the bene fits. It is a major asset for New Zealand because it will
generate huge benefits—a projected $90 million annual injection into this economy, and
that is an estimated 1,000 jobs. [ Interruption] I challenge those opposite to come to
Skycity and say to the bouncers down at Skycity—those who have jobs and are
supporting families and are supporting their wives, families, spouses—that they want to
talk to them about their jobs and about taking the jobs away from those people who
have them. I challenge those members opposite to do that.
The 230 new pokie machines is only the same amount that was produced under the
Labour Government. I acknowledge the Hon Tre vor Mallard, who has actually said in
this House that he did make a mistake under th at legislation. I challenge others to make
the same statement, because they are, in effect, voting against something that they voted
for 10 years ago. But let us talk about the facts, because members opposite do not want
11 Jul 2013 New Zealand Internatio nal Convention Centre Bill 11989
to talk about the facts. Under Labour there were 6,700 extra pokie machines in 9
years—6,700—and under National we have d ecreased the number of machines in
circulation around this country by 2,300. So we have decreased the ability for harm to
be caused by decreasing accessibility to those machines for those who are being harmed
by these machines by decreasing the number of machines across this country.
What are the measures to deter problem ga mbling at Skycity? Well, we know that it
is introducing a predictive modelling tool, which analyses data to identify those
gamblers with problems. It is also in troducing player identification requirements—
[Interruption] members know that—and some of t hose will be visual identification
requirements. But it is a balanc ing act, as I said at the outse t. Overall, the net benefits
are positive for our economy, positive for our country, and positive for those who are
getting jobs under this legislation. That is why I will support it in its first reading.

items.speaker: RICHARD PROSSER
items.text: I rise on behalf of New Zealand First to speak to
this first reading of the New Zealand International Convention Centre Bill. New
Zealand First opposes this bill and everythi ng it stands for unequi vocally and in its
entirety. We oppose this bill because it epitomises everything that is wrong about core
governance of a nation from an economic standpoint, from  an ideological standpoint,
from a social good standpoint, and, perhaps as important as—if not, indeed, more so
than—any of those, from the standpoint of  the voluntary adherenc e by the Government
of the day to the otherwise unenforceab le, yet constitutionally fundamental and
indispensable, convention by which those who hold executive office choose to maintain
their subservience to the laws of the land, choose to maintain the ethos by which laws
are made and upheld in accordance with the principles of democracy and the best
interests of the common good, and choose to conduct themselves and to execute their
responsibilities of their offi ce in a manner uncorrupted by the temptations of material
gain or regulatory and jurisdictional advantage—or not. They choose to conduct
themselves and to carry out th e business of Government in th is manner, or they choose
to not do that.
When Governments choose to depart from these fundamental conventions, it is the
beginning of an insidious process of thought and the beginning of a very dangerous road
that leads towards corruption and at the end of which lie the remains of societies that
have traded democracy for the usurpation of power. It is a road that begins in the
corruption of thought and ends in dictatorshi p. Fiji lies at the end of that road. So do
Zimbabwe, Pakistan, and Egypt—only this month, Egypt. Half the nations of South
America and West Africa have gone down that road, and none of them have ever truly
come back. Is that what we want for New Z ealand? Is that what we are going to allow?
Is that what we are going to sanction for New Zealand—for the future of New
Zealand—here in this House by passing this cynical and insidious piece of legislation? I
say that in all seriousness. I ask all members, but partic ularly the members opposite on
the Government benches, the members of the National Party, whether that is what they
really want, and whether that is what they really want to allow.
I say again that this bill is the beginning of  a process that culminates in the ending of
democracy, and I suspect that those who are responsible for initia ting it are not even
aware that it is happening. I make this char ge because this bill sends a message, and I
make it because of what this bill is and what it does and what it represents, and because
of the message this bill sends. What it says is  that the law is for sale. The law here in
New Zealand and the process of making law is for sale. Make us an offer, and we will
change the law to suit! The Government can spin  this any way it likes. It can dress it up
any way it likes. It can plaster that pig with  as much lipstick as it can stagger under the
weight of, but the reality remains the same, and that reality is that our laws are for sale.
11990 New Zealand International Conve ntion Centre Bill 11 Jul 2013
We have laws limiting the activity of gambling. We have laws that limit gambling
and place limits on how much gambling can  go on and where and when and by whom.
We have them because gambling can, and does, cause harm, and as a society we have
decided that we need to be able to limit that  harm. We believe as a society that it is in
the best interests of the comm on good to see to it that th e harm that can be caused by
gambling is minimised. Yet, through this b ill, that impetus towards harm minimisation
is being abandoned. Through this bill, with this bill, what we  are doing—what New
Zealand is doing, what the Government is doi ng, and what the Parliament is allowing to
happen—is that we are deciding, arbitrarily, that the minimisation of gambling and the
minimisation of the harm and the potential  harm caused by gambling is not important
any more. It is not as important as some other considerations—economic
considerations, monetary considerations. Jobs  are important. On that , I think we are all
agreed. Industry and building and construction are important . No one is denying that.
We need jobs for people. We need building and construction and major projects in the
economy. That goes without saying.
But within that reality is another reality, and it is this. Even wh en we as a nation
acknowledge that we need jobs  and industry and c onstruction, we still have this other
reality, which is that we have problems with gambling in this country. We have problem
gamblers and we have harm being done, and th at is why we have laws pertaining to
gambling. They are there in an attempt to mi nimise that harm, but through this bill, the
Government is denying that reality. The Government is attempting to justify the
changes in this law by referring to the jobs that will be created by the construction of the
new convention centre and by re ferring to the revenue that  it anticipates will be
generated in the economy by having the c onvention centre operating and from the
overseas visitors whom it will attract. And it is true that those things will happen.
Building a convention centre will create jobs and it will inject new revenue into our
economy, but that is not good enough. There are other ways  in which jobs can be
created and there are other ways in which Crown revenues can be enlarged.
Does Auckland actually need another c onvention centre? Have we as a nation
actually asked that question? Auckland al ready has the Aotea Centre, of course.
Whether having another one as a crucial element in the Queen City remaining
competitive with the other 70-odd convention ve nues in our region is a matter for some
contention. But if we do, in fact, need another one, someone has to build it and someone
has to pay for it. So the question then is whether we should,  as a nation and a
Parliament, be changing the law in order to  allow Skycity to build one for us free of
charge in exchange for their being allowe d to expand their casino by an additional 230
pokie machines and another 35 gaming tables. Does Auckland or New Zealand need
another 230 pokie machines? I would contend that they do not.
It is true that some people use pokies responsibly and gain some enjoyment from
doing that. But it is equally true that these machines are designed to make a profit, and
that is what they do. Eight-five cents of  every dollar that goe s into a pokie, or
thereabouts, stays in that machine. They are programmed and built that way. There is no
getting away from that, but people play them anyway, because they are fun and
exciting, and they come with the promise of reward, and that promise can be, and often
is, addictive. As such, these machines have  become a scourge in our pubs and suburbs
and communities. We have problem gamblers in this country—far more of them than
many people would care to admit. It is not a problem that is restricted to the poorer parts
of New Zealand or to brown people or to the less well educated. Gambling addiction
cuts across all socio-economic levels and all strata of so ciety, all ethnic groups, and all
levels of income.
11 Jul 2013 New Zealand Internatio nal Convention Centre Bill 11991
I have had firsthand experience of being in a relationship with someone who was
unable to resist the temptation of putting anot her coin in the machine. I watched as my
best efforts to assist failed and a person who held a good job in a position of
responsibility succumbed to her affliction just as progressively and just as destructively
as the damage and decline experienced by an untreated alcohol ic or drug addict.
Gambling addiction destroys lives. It ru ins livelihoods, it breaks up families, and it
breaks up relationships. It is a horrible thing to watch and an even more horrible thing to
experience. We do not need 230 more pokie machines. We need 230 fewer, and that
would be a good start.
We most certainly do not need to tear dow n laws that have been put in place to
protect the vulnerable because we have succumbed to the temptation of a promise of
$400 million in the form of a convention ce ntre. This windfall win, as it is being
perceived and promoted, is no less a mirage than any other win on the pokies. Has this
Government, I ask, been seduced by the prom ise of the bright lights and the flashing
colours and the big dollars to be had from this exciting casino deal? I ask because there
is a common thread. There is a common set of indicators in people with addictions.
Drugs, alcohol, gambling—they are all the sa me. One of the most common early signs
is denial accompanied by justification and minimisation. Smokers begin that way and so
do drinkers. They say: “Just one more puff. Just one more beer. Go on, have a chaser
with that. One more won’t kill you. Everyone else is doing it. The sun is always over
the yardarm somewhere in the world. Just one  more twenty. Ten more coins and that’s
it. I’m not feeding the pokies anymore this we ek—well, tonight.” It starts that way and
then every subsequent indulgence is justified by the one before it, and then there is full-
blown addiction and a cycle of self-destr uction that is inescapable. There is
minimisation, justification, and denial. The ps ychology of addiction is very similar to
the psychology of the corruption of thought.
Is there a parallel here? I ask the House and the members opposite to ask themselves
whether that is, indeed, what they are doing and whether this is what is happening with
their thinking: “Just one  little law change, that’s all. Just a few more pokies. Think of
the jobs. Think of the investment. Just one little law change. Go on, it won’t hurt.” I ask
them to contemplate that, because do you know  what? Once they have done it, the next
time it will be so much easier—so much easier to do and so much easier to justify. They
might say: “What law shall we sell next, I wonder?”.
The Prime Minister obviously understands the maxim that one should never gamble
with more than one can afford to lose, and that is why he is wh ipping his caucus and
their individual consciences into line. But I ask those members whether they have the
intestinal fortitude to do the right thing here  today, rather than the thing they have been
told to do. If they vote to sell this law t oday, how will they justify not wanting to sell
another one tomorrow? We are at a fork in the road. One way is the right way. At the
end of the other is Zimbabwe. We all have a choice as to which road we will take and
which way we will vote. We must live with the consequences of that choice.
I will be voting against this bill, as w ill my New Zealand First colleagues. I would
urge the members opposite to choose very carefully whether they support this law or not
and to vote accordingly while they still have th at free choice in a free society. Thank
you.

items.speaker: KANWALJIT SINGH BAKSHI
items.text: Sat sri akaal, Mr Assistant Speaker.
Thank you very much for the opportunity to pa rticipate in the firs t reading of the New
Zealand International Convention Centre Bill. I congratulate this John Key - led
Government on achieving an agreement that is way better than what our Opposition
predecessors tried to achieve in  2001. I am sure others have shared this to some degree
earlier today. However, just to re-emphasise, this agreement that the National-led
11992 New Zealand International Conve ntion Centre Bill 11 Jul 2013
Government has formed with Skycity is better for the economy, better for Auckland,
and better for New Zealand. With my clear  conscience, I commend this bill to the
House.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I understand the ne xt call is a split
call. The Hon David Parker—5 minutes.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: Thank you, Mr Assist ant Speaker. I would
appreciate a bell at 1 minute, if I could?

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: Thank you. This is the result of a backroom deal by our
Prime Minister, done with vested interests.
Le’aufa’amulia Asenati Lole-Taylor: It was a dirty one too.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: A dirty one, someone says here. The Deputy Auditor-
General inquired into the probity of this  arrangement. I want to quote a couple of
paragraphs from the Deputy Auditor-Gener al’s report because we heard continual
misrepresentation, including by National members today, that it was all in order. The
Deputy Auditor-General concluded in the re port that was done by one of her deputies
that “The result was that one submitter was treated differently fr om others during the
evaluation process.” Only one bidder for this project knew that regulatory holidays were
available. Only one bidder knew that the G overnment was willing to change the laws so
that they could get a break. No other bidder knew that, and that is why the Deputy
Auditor-General concluded that this process was wrong.
That fundamental error was never fixed, a nd we will never know  whether, had the
prospect of regulatory holidays been conve yed to other bidders, we would have had
others. There are lots of rumours around that  Vector would have been interested in
bidding. It faced regulatory risk around the revenues that it gets from its lines
businesses. Vector may have been willing to  subsidise a convention centre if it had
certainty as to its revenue flows and if it had a regulatory change that took away its risks
in the way this regulatory change being done for Skycity does.
There is another really shady thing going in here. There is a pretence by National that
it was not warned. We know from the Deputy Auditor-General’s report—and again I am
reading from it—that “The Treasury … noted that an important part of the standard PPP
process was a market tender, which provided assurance that the taxpayer was receiving
value for money. … Overall, the Treasury co mments suggested that  officials should
think about other, more conventional, procurement approaches.” The Treasury
comments were referred to in an email of 12 November 2009 that went to the
Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet from the Ministry of Economic
Development. Treasury comments went to the Ministry of Economic Development,
then from the Ministry of  Economic Development to the Department of the Prime
Minister and Cabinet, and then  the Department of the Prim e Minister and Cabinet, in
addition, wrote a briefing note to the Prime Minister. None of those documents has been
disclosed. Are we such a corrupt country that  we cannot see what warnings were given
to the Government by the Civil Service?
I raised this very issue with Steven Joyce when he was at the Finance and
Expenditure Committee on estimates for th e Ministry of Business, Innovation and
Employment the other day. He said that they would be released in due course when the
other documents were released. I checked to day. They still have not been disclosed,
because this seedy, underhand, irresponsible, di sreputable deal is wrong and these notes
from the Government departments to the G overnment told it that it was wrong. So, in
addition to all of the problems with this ca sino deal—it is a casino deal; it is not a
convention centre deal—that resu lts in a convention centre being built on the back of
gambling harm, the Government knew it was wrong for reasons other than gambling
11 Jul 2013 New Zealand Internatio nal Convention Centre Bill 11993
harm. New Zealand’s reputation as being a transparent country free of corruption is
tarnished by this deal, and that tarnish cannot be undone.
I want to say a couple of other things. No Parliament can curb the sovereignty of a
future Parliament. That means that futu re measures to remedy gambling harm are
always within the jurisdiction of a future Parliament. We in the Labour Party say that
we reserve the right to legislate for gambling harm in the future. That does not mean to
say that that will be without cost to ta xpayers. This deal with the Government
effectively promises compensation to Skycity  in respect of some future steps by a
Government, and not all of that could be avoided by a future Government, despite the
fact that future Governments might want to go the whole hog and reverse everything.
That would come at a cost. But make no mist ake: future Governments have a right to
regulate for gambling harm. This bill reflects poorly upon the Government and I for one
will be opposing it.

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: I rise and speak as a resi dent of Auckland, but also
a resident of central Auckland, the place where this eventual convention centre will
reside. I rise also as someone who lives in the area where Skycity is the most significant
employer in terms of numbers. It was absolutely irresponsible of that member opposite
to claim that not building a convention centre under the auspices of Skycity would have
led people who are currently employed to lo sing their jobs. That was an outrageous
statement to make. It is also outrageous to try to claim that this  was the only option on
the table. Let us not be naive. Labour has been opposed to this casino deal from the
beginning. We have never been opposed to a convention centre being built. There is a
very important, distinct difference there. Of course this side of the House wants to see
decent economic development. Of course this side of the House wants to see Auckland
thrive, tourism grow, and people being offere d opportunities that a potential convention
centre could bring. Did we want that to ha ppen off the back of harm and misery? No,
and that is why we oppose this deal.
Also, we cannot be naive and pretend that th is was the only offer on the table. That
seems to have been somewhat lost in this de bate. In fact, before the Prime Minister had
a chat with Skycity and realised  that it was interested to the point that it might not cost
him a pretty penny, there were several othe r deals on the table, including one from
Ngāti Whātua and another from The Edge. Auckland Council put forward a proposition
that we had the Aotea Centre , which could be better utilis ed, and we could expand the
footprint of that centre. We c ould transport the arts side of  the Aotea Centre to the St
James—a beautiful jewel in the Auckland crown that is in desperate need of restoration.
It is something that the people of Auckland ha ve been crying out to happen for years,
and, while it sits and crumbles in the cen tre of Auckland, we had a proposition on the
table that could have seen a beautiful trad e-off that would have allowed a convention
centre and for that jewel in the crown of  Auckland to be restored. Instead, the
Government bought a crown of coin machines for Auckland. That was the trade-off that
that Government decided to make.
I have been interested in the debate that  we have recently seen around inequality.
According to the OECD measures, the Gini  coefficient, New Zealand is the most
unequal it has ever been. One of the points th at the IMF makes around inequality is that
countries that live with deep  inequality tend to have Governments that start making
decisions on behalf of those who are most powerful rather than on behalf of the good of
the country and the economy, and that is exactly what this d eal represents. It was made
on behalf of those who are powerful rather than those who cannot vote—in particular,
kids. The Expert Advisory Group on Solutions to Child Poverty points out that problem
gambling is correlated with child poverty, and, in fact, it exacerbates it. That is a point
that has been made time and time again by the Problem Gambling Foundation and any
expert who works on child poverty issues. If  you want to support those who are most
11994 New Zealand International Conve ntion Centre Bill 11 Jul 2013
vulnerable, you do everything you can to remo ve problem gambling and, in particular,
pokie machines.
Any Government that argues that it is ha ppy to simply minimise harm, I think, is
making a ridiculous argument. It is like saying that you w ould rather raise the speed
limit, knowing people would die, and then simply minimise the harm by putting more
gurneys in a hospital. It is a flawed argument, and it is a point  that is right to have been
made before now. Any Government that argues  it would rather make that trade-off is
trying to put power before people. This co mes back to my main point. This deal
demonstrates, I believe, the stark differe nce between National and Labour. We both
want jobs—yes. We both want economic de velopment—yes. But Labour would have
conducted an open and transparen t process that would ensure  a convention centre that
was a place of pride, not harm, and was about people, not pokies.

items.speaker: Dr JIAN YANG
items.text: Here is what Auckland Tourism, Events and Economic
Development Chief Executive Mr Brett O’R iley has to say rega rding the convention
centre: “We are delighted with the opportunities  this will bring to the region. It will
allow Auckland to compete strongly against ot her international cities and secure major

Executive Phil O’Reilly said: “New Zealand, as one of the most remote tourism

good deal for New Zealand. It will create jobs, boost tourism, and bring significant

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I understand that the next call is a
split call.
Su’a WILLIAM SIO (Labour—Māngere): I rise to take a call on the New Zealand
International Convention Centre Bill, the Government bill here. I want to appeal to the
House to put politics aside a nd do the right thi ng for the community. The people of
Māngere strongly oppose the bill for the following reason: the harm of gambling is real.
11 Jul 2013 New Zealand Internatio nal Convention Centre Bill 11995
Le’aufa’amulia Asenati Lole-Taylor: In Manukau East?
Su’a WILLIAM SIO: Absolutely. I dare say my colleague there is absolutely right.
Throughout Manukau, the feeling is the sa me. Throughout the Manukau region, the
feeling is that the harm is real. Any member in this House who believes that it is not real
is either blind or just ignorant of the reality out there in our community. All they need to
do is talk to the Salvation Army. All they need to do is talk with the communities on the
ground that are having to deal with the harm. People in this House need to know that the
sole reason for the existence of casinos and pokie machines is to exploit and prey on the
vulnerable. They make money, but not for the community.
Let me just read out part of the regu latory impact statement given to the

items.speaker: Government
items.text: “The key concern … is the poten tial impact this may have in increasing
the incidence of problem gambling and its a ssociated harm for New Zealand society. …
Research shows there is a clear link between  the availability of gaming machines and
opportunities to gamble and the incidence of problem gambling.” The region of
Manukau has always known this. In 2003 we carried out research into the social harm
on the people of Manukau, and the research revealed that $91 million was what it cost
that region each year in terms of the social effects of gamb ling. It also said that the
number of people affected by problem ga mbling is virtually unknown, although it is
about 15 to 20 percent of the population. By  and large, it is a hidden problem. But
Australian research found that the net gain in jobs and economic activity from gambling
is small, as the money involved is simply being diverted from spending in other areas.
Again, the Australian research showed that  the national cost of problem gambling is
greater than the taxes raised by the Government from gambling activities.
As my colleague Trevor Mallard said earli er, it does impact on family relationships.
It does impact on people losing their homes. It has impact on people—some commit
suicide because they have lost virtually everyt hing. It is addictive. Despite what we say,
that there are avenues to help problem gamblers, the reality is true that those avenues
are just not helping our communities. It is wrong for this Government and for any future
Government to think that by increasing cas inos we can provide benefits to the
community. It has been argued that jobs are created—certain ly. But the reality is that
these are low-value, low-pa id jobs, and that is not the kind of New Zealand the
community wants. The community deserves quality jobs. The community deserves a
living wage. That is what the public have been arguing for.
Again, I would appeal, particularly to the Government members, to put politics aside
and do the right thing. The way is open fo r you to conduct a conscience vote, and I
would ask members, particularly those who live in the Manukau region—Peseta Sam
Lotu-Iiga, Alfred Ngaro, and Claudette Haui ti—to do the right thing for the community
and vote against this bill. I would ask them to use their conscience. I know that Jami-
Lee Ross does not have a conscience, and I know that Mr Baks hi will not have a
conscience. They are going to vote in support of  this bill, despite the harm that happens
in our community.
But the most important thing—and members of the House will be fully aware of
this—is that this a bad, sti nky deal, hatched and consumma ted on the dinner tables at
Skycity. Like my other colleagues have said , this is a deal that undermines the
credibility of this country of ours. In passi ng this bill, what this Government does is it
ushers in a new, dark era of dirty politics with its mates. I will be voting against this bill.

items.speaker: DENISE ROCHE
items.text: T ēnā koe. T ēnā koutou e te Whare. I rise to take the
second call for the Greens on the New Zealand International Convention Centre Bill. It
is no secret that we have been opposed to this bill since we first uncovered the dodgy
dealings that have resulted in the legislation we are discussing today. The Greens have a
proud history of opposing mining on schedule 4 land, opposing deep-s ea oil drilling,
and opposing fracking, and we oppose this deal because it favours another nasty
11996 New Zealand International Conve ntion Centre Bill 11 Jul 2013
extraction industry, one that hoovers money out  of the pockets of those who can least
afford it, and, just like the worst frackers, it le aves a hell of a mess. We all live with the
consequences and we all bear the costs.
And what are the costs? Well, we do not know. We have some clues. The regulatory
impact statement says that there will be increased problem gambling from the 230 extra
pokies and more tables. There will be increas ed risk of suicide and domestic violence.
There will be more kids going hungry and kids  being neglected and left in cars. We
know that there will be increas ed crime as a result of in creased gambling opportunities.
We know that there will be more thefts of businesses and charities to fuel gambling. We
know that there will be more gangs, more P dealers, and even some international
criminals laundering their money at the extended casino.
In terms of cost-benefit analysis, that really has not been done. The Government
keeps stating that there will be jobs and there will be benefits to the economy, but,
actually, the losses and the social harms that we will all pay for have not been factored
into the equation. I ask the Government to do the maths. I query the overstated
economic benefits. The research undertaken by the Australian Productivity Commission
shows that casinos suck the money out of the surrounding areas and take it away from
restaurants, from theatres, from shops, and the surrounding area. It will basically
concentrate all that money at the Skycity venue.
Yesterday I went to a talk by Robert Wade, from the London School of Economics
and Political Science. He was talking about in equality. He showed a graph representing
the ever-widening income gap between the ve ry rich and the very poor, and showed
how most of the wealth in A nglo countries is concentrated  with the wealthy. Here, the
top 1 percent of income earners own 16 percent of New Zealand’s total wealth,
compared with the bottom 50 percent, who own just 5 percent of the wealth. He
explains how this comes about  by the policy directions th at Governments take that
ensure that wealth stays w ith the wealthy. He talked about the money empathy gap,
where those who benefit from the Governme nt policy directions, who have lots of
money, develop less empathy for those with out money, considering those on low
incomes even as feckless. He also talked about the need to get rid of the big money
from the political system, and to stop po litical parties taking donations from big
businesses. Does that sound familiar?
This legislation illustrates ve ry, very clearly everything he said. We have a deal on
the table here that will deliver a convention centre in Auckland and it will increase
inequality in Aotearoa New Zealand. We do not  have to do this deal. We really do not.
If we really need a convention centre, publicly funding this would cost in the vicinity of
$20 million per year over 35 years.  That equates to less than  $10 per year per taxpayer.
We would own that convention centre. We would control that c onvention centre. We
would avoid the increased social harm that will certainly come with it under the Skycity
arrangement. We would also avoid a 35-year compensation clause that
unconstitutionally chains future Governments to providing profits for Skycity Casino’s
shareholders. I call on all MPs across this House to ditch this bill.

items.speaker: MARK MITCHELL
items.text: Every single day New Zealand is in
competition with the rest of the world. Every single day visitors are getting on planes to
go and visit other parts of the world, and we are part of that competition every day. New
Zealand needs an international convention ce ntre. We are too small to stand still. I
commend this New Zealand International Convention Centre Bill to the House.

items.speaker: Hon TODD McCLAY
items.text: I move, That the
Psychoactive Substances Bill be now read a third time . It is my hope that today we take
a very significant step to protect New Zealanders, par ticularly young New Zealanders,
from the harm caused by untested drugs and an unregulated market. The Government’s
position is clear, as I believe this Hous e’s is. No one will be allowed to sell
psychoactive products unless it can be shown that those pro ducts pose no more than a
low risk of harm. Passing this bill will ensu re that these products cannot be sold to
children, that they cannot be sold from dairie s, and that there are robust controls on
what is in them and how they can be marketed.
Normally, I would take 10 minutes in this  debate, but as we go into the school
holidays it is my concern that there are pr oducts there on our wharve s that are going to
flood the New Zealand market, to be used to create a black market, and to drop prices in
supermarkets. I will not speak for a singl e moment longer in this House and put
children’s lives at risk. I commend this bill to the House.

items.speaker: IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY
items.text: This is a great day. Our
communities up and down New Zealand will be celebrating because this is the day that
we legislate to get drugs out of dairies, a nd I have to say that it has been a long time
coming. I am appalled by that Government over there, which has prioritised creating
more opportunities to gamble and increasing th e harm related to gambling ahead of this
legislation, the Psychoactive S ubstances Bill, which is desi gned to reduce drug-related
harm. That is a shocking indictment on that  Government’s priorities, and it saddens me.
It saddens me that this excellent piece of  legislation, which communities have been
waiting for, which people working in the drug and alcohol treatment sector have been
waiting for, and which, indeed, the people work ing in this industry who want to see a
regulated, smart, cowboy-free industry have been waiting for for so very long. And once
again—this has been the theme of this legisl ation and the way that this Government has
managed this legislation—we are rushing it.
We are rushing one of the most worthwhile pieces of legislation that have appeared
in the world of drug regulation in a very long time. This G overnment places such a low
11 Jul 2013 Psychoactive Substances Bill 12001
priority on reducing drug-related ha rm that it is rushing it in  the last minute in the last
hour before we go on a 2-week adjournment. It is an outrage. It is an outrage that the
Government puts such a low priority on keepi ng our children safe that it is rushing this
legislation. Every moment of this process has been rushed. The Government left it for 2
long years after the Law Commission presen ted its recommendations. The Government
brought this legislation to the House in Febr uary, and it sat on the Table for month after
month after month, sitting way down on the Order Paper because there were other
things that were more important to this G overnment than reducing the harm related to
drugs. Then the Government made us rush the select committee process. We could not
hear all the submitters, and we did not have time to get everything right. Then the
Associate Minister of Health Todd McClay presents amendments handwritten at the last
minute of the Committee stage.
And then we get to today. We are selli ng legislation to Skycity. Binding future
Parliaments to not be able to address gambling-related harm is an issue of greater
priority to the National Government than reducing drug-related harm. That is an
outrage.

items.speaker: Melissa Lee
items.text: Calm down.

items.speaker: IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY
items.text: That Government should hang its head in shame.
Melissa Lee wants me to drop my voice. I will not drop my voice. I am angry at you,
Melissa Lee. I am angry at that Government because that Government does not have the
interests of our communities at heart. That  is why I am shouting, Melissa Lee, because
this could have been great le gislation. This could have been  a marvellous step forward
for drug regulation in New Zealand. This c ould have been the opportunity to not only
get the drugs out of our dairies but also create for the first time a legal, regulated market
designed to reduce the harm associated with dr ugs. It will do that, but the attitude this
Government has taken is just appalling. It ha s dithered, it has wasted time, and here we
are, rushing this thr ough right after that Government ha s voted to increase harm to our
communities by allowing more gambling and selling off legislation to a corporation—
outrageous.
I do support this legislation. I think it is a good bill. It  has been a very long time
coming. I am pleased that members around the House have seen through some of the
distractions and the things that have divided us to eventually get to a piece of legislation
that we can all support. Although this does do th e job of getting the drugs out of dairies,
there are a few things that could have been done  better. One of those is to deal with the
issue of possession. This is about creating a regulated ma rket and ensuring that the
manufacturers and sellers of high-risk substa nces get everything that they deserve, and
that those who continue to flout the law get everything that they deserve. That is where
we should be focusing our attention, not on the young people who find themselves in
possession of these substances. It does nothing to advance the cause of this legislation to
make the possession of an unapproved substanc e an offence, and it does nothing to fine
those people. In fact, it will be an abso lutely unenforceable component of this
legislation. So I hope that in the future we will see fit to decriminalise the possession of
these substances.
The other thing I am concerned about is th e new transition peri od that the Minister
dumped on the Table at the very last minute. The Minister who was not the originator of
the bill, the Minister who took no part in the select committe e process, and the Minister
who is a johnny-come-lately to this legislation and dumped at the very last minute a
change to the transition period. It is a tran sition period that was deliberately designed to
avoid a black market. I have noticed that the National Party has been throwing around
today the idea that a black market might be created. The only thing that will create a
black market is prohibition. My fear is that  because we did not ha ve time to properly
12002 Psychoactive Substances Bill 11 Jul 2013
consider all the consequen ces and unintended conseque nces of the Minister’s
amendment, what we may discover is that by reducing that transition period down to 3
months a black market is precisely what th e result will be. I am hoping that is not the
case. I am hoping that the Minist er is right, and that the manufacture rs of substances
that are up for approval will be able to prove within that 3-month period that they have
made some steps towards initiating clinical tr ials and that the Minister will then see fit
to allow those substances to stay on the shelf, because what is really important is that
the low-risk substances do stay  in the regulated legal market. The last thing we want to
do is create a black market by having effect ive prohibition being the result of this
legislation.
One of the aspects of this Psychoactive Subs tances Bill is a review after a maximum
of 5 years. That is a good idea given that this is in novative and world-leading
legislation. We need to have a review after 5 years to see whether we have got it right.
There are a couple of things th at I think are absolutely nece ssary in that review, if not
before. The first is to consider the possib ility of applying an excise tax to these
substances. It is what we do with tobacco. It  is what we do with alcohol. It is a good
way of, one, raising revenue to fund the addic tion services that may be needed to deal
with the problems relating to these and other substances, and, two, using price as a
demand-limiting control. We failed to do that with the alcohol legislation. We do it very
well with tobacco. I think it should be applied to these substances as well. But I
appreciate that we need to ha ve a look at the pricing points and we need to look at what
the appropriate way of using an excise tax is.
Finally, what I want to see is what the Law Commission actually originally
envisaged, and that is a comprehensive revi ew of the Misuse of Drugs Act. It is
outdated. It is outmoded. It may have been ap propriate in 1975, but it is not appropriate
in 2013. In fact, the Misuse of Drugs Act is doing more harm than good in the 21 st
century. All we have done here is actually cr eate an added layer. So now we will have
some high-risk substances that  are legal, some high-risk s ubstances that are illegal,
some low-risk substances that are legal, and so me low-risk substances that are illegal. If
that sounds confusing to peop le, it is because it is. Ou r drug legislati on is utterly
confusing, and what we really need is—better than this, more than this—a true review
of the Misuse of Drugs Act. But for now, because this bill will get the—

items.text: Given the exigencies of time, my
call will be a brief one. I do not  need to feign my delight th is afternoon as the author

and can I acknowledge the support of the H ouse. This is a good day for New Zealand
communities, and that is something the previous speaker and I do agree on. Many
11 Jul 2013 Psychoactive Substances Bill 12003
